I'm joined in the studio right now with Michelle Roy, who's sort of becoming a sidekick with the Holo Talk Show.
Oh, thank you.
The trustee sidekick, like Batman and Robin.
Batman and Robin, yeah, Frank and Michelle.
Okay.
We have a number of special broadcasts that's coming up for you over the next few weeks.
We visited the Center for Holographic Arts in New York City, actually Queens, right?
That's where it was.
And uh they had their opening there with a number of their artists in residency uh program students works that were on display.
And we had an opportunity to interview a number of the people who were uh represented in that show.
So over the next few weeks we're going to be uh bringing you uh these programs, and Michelle uh joined me in New York City to uh interview them as well.
And Michelle, I have no idea what I want to ask you.
Well that should work well.
Basically, why don't you tell the listeners we know you've been on the Holo Talk Show before you do a special on careers?
Um, why don't you take a minute to uh tell the listeners what it is that we'll be doing together when we do programs together.
What do you mean?
Well ask me that question differently.
Say for instance someone comes to see us do a program.
What would it be?
What would this be when they come to see us?
My interest in all of this is uh related to um careers and lasers and holography and photonics is in terms of um how they can turn into careers for people.

So for example, when we went to uh Queens yesterday, uh you were talking to people about more of the, you know, technical aspect of what they were doing and um the artistic uh pieces of it, although I like to talk about the artistic parts too.
Uh but you did a very nice job.
Oh, thank you.
Yes.
Thank you.
But my uh major interest is in w what makes someone want to do this, what makes someone want to go into uh holography, what kinds of mental disorders.
Exact exactly.
Trying to identify mental disorders.
I was I am trying to hook people up with some psychiatric, you know, resources if necessary.
No, just you know, finding out what what interests people about the field, what do they enjoy about the field, what kinds of opportunities are out there.

Uh some of the people that we spoke with yesterday talked about like internship possibilities and uh artists in residence programs and so forth, classes that you can take that, you know, let people who are interested in pursuing it a little more uh deeply have an opportunity to get some different kinds of experiences and if they want to turn it into a career, then you know, there there would be a way to do that.

So that was more my take on um what what we were doing and and why we were there, which when we do programs together, that's where I fill in as well is looking at how people can turn what is obviously a passion.
I mean that came through loud and clear in all of the interviews that we did yesterday that people do this because they really love it.
Um and I'm in a b a big believer in um taking the things that you really love to do, figuring out how to make some money off of it.
So you know, that's basically uh sort of the approach I was taking.
Do you think people basically mention their passion because they don't make a lot of money?
I'm sure that's part of it.

I mean, particularly I mean we were talking to artists, so you know, um people who are are not using lasers in like an industrial setting or something like that where it might be a little bit different and you have business driving it so that there is money.
Um, yeah, I would say that those people probably, you know, they have to be driven by something because it's it certainly wasn't money, um, that it is, you know, the love of the field.

Well see the thing that I thought was interesting about yesterday was I I am more in many ways more aware of you know lasers in terms of using it in communications and that sort of thing, more of that business kind of field.
And the thing that was fun about yesterday was talking to people who are artists, you know, and who use you know who who really see the hologram as the thing.
Yeah.
Um so that was just sort of a different, you know, perspective.
Yeah.
And holography is a great way to get people to come in and experience lasers.
Sure, right.
Yeah, I mean you could bring someone into a classroom or someone into a workshop and just teach them about lasers.
But holography is a wonderful way to combine a lot of different elements of learning and at the same time l allow them to get experience with lasers.
And so much more constructive than shining laser pens in.
Uh we have a program coming up where you can come and see Michelle and I at the Smithsonian on May 6th.
And uh we're going to have an exhibit of holograms there, and we'll be doing uh presentations throughout the day.
At the Hershawn Museum.
At the Hershawn Museum uh of the Smithsonian, which is right on the mall.
And uh we'll have more information on that as uh time goes on.

But uh over the next few weeks you're going to be hearing some programs that Michelle and I put together while we were in New York and that will sort of lead us up to the uh the programs that we will be running at the Smithsonian in Washington coming up on May 6th, and that's the program for uh for the public.
We also have another program coming up for uh a national teachers conference that will be there as well.

Michelle, thank you very much for uh coming into the studio and going on the trip.

A new show each week.
Don't forget to tune in.
See ya.
See ya.

With this is our very first exhibition uh for the artists uh who received the Artists in Residency program.

We this is our second year and we are funded for one more yeah and after that we hope to continue to be funded further but we don't know yet.
